items.followUp: Define a polyatomic ion and give one example.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of a molecular ion.
rubric.description: Defines a molecular ion as a group of bonded atoms carrying a net charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a group of atoms and its charge.

rubric.why: Checks the difference in electrical charge.
rubric.description: States that a molecule is neutral, whereas a molecular ion has a net charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each side of the comparison, up to 2.

rubric.why: Checks a consequence of the ion's charge.
rubric.description: Distinguishes their behaviour in an electric field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a molecular ion is deflected or moves in an electric field, unlike a neutral molecule.

rubric.why: Checks suitable examples and charge notation.
rubric.description: Gives examples of a molecule and a molecular ion, with the ion's charge shown.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct paired example.

modelAnswer: A molecular ion is a group of two or more covalently bonded atoms that carries a net positive or negative charge and behaves as a single ion.
A molecule is electrically neutral; a molecular ion has a net charge.
A molecule has equal total positive and negative charges; a molecular ion has an imbalance between them.
A neutral molecule is not deflected by an electric field; a charged molecular ion is deflected.
A molecule is written without a charge, for example H₂O; a molecular ion is written with its charge, for example NH₄⁺.

items.followUp: Draw and label a discharge tube, and explain how cathode rays are produced.

rubric.why: Checks the essential labelled features of the discharge-tube diagram.
rubric.description: Shows a low-pressure gas tube with an anode, a perforated cathode, and canal rays passing through the cathode holes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the labelled electrodes and gas tube, and 1 mark for showing the rays passing through the holes.

rubric.why: Checks the conditions and nature of canal-ray production.
rubric.description: Explains that a high-voltage discharge through low-pressure gas produces positively charged particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the discharge to positive particles.

rubric.why: Checks the path and identification of the rays.
rubric.description: States that positive particles pass through the perforations in the cathode to form canal rays; hydrogen gas produces protons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the path through the cathode holes or for identifying hydrogen canal rays as protons.

modelAnswer: Diagram (not to scale):
[Anode (+)]   → positive canal rays →   [perforated cathode (−), with holes]
low-pressure gas in a glass discharge tube; high voltage applied across the electrodes
The tube contains gas at low pressure and a high voltage is applied across its electrodes.
The discharge ionises the gas atoms, producing positively charged particles and electrons.
The positive particles move towards the cathode and pass through its perforations, forming canal rays.
When the gas is hydrogen, the positive particles are H⁺ ions (protons).

items.followUp: State five physical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Checks a characteristic appearance of metals.
rubric.description: States that metals are generally lustrous or shiny.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

rubric.why: Checks the ability of metals to be shaped.
rubric.description: States that metals are malleable and can be beaten into sheets.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

rubric.why: Checks the ability of metals to be drawn into wires.
rubric.description: States that metals are ductile.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

rubric.why: Checks the characteristic conductivity of metals.
rubric.description: States that metals conduct heat and electricity well; another valid general property may be given for the second mark.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for good electrical conductivity and 1 mark for good thermal conductivity or another valid property such as sonority or high melting point.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous (shiny).
They are malleable and can be beaten into thin sheets.
They are ductile and can be drawn into wires.
They are good conductors of heat and electricity.
They are generally sonorous and have high melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: Describe the Tyndall effect and state how it helps identify a colloid.

rubric.why: Checks the nature of a colloid.
rubric.description: States that a colloid is heterogeneous, even if it may appear uniform.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

rubric.why: Checks the characteristic size range of colloidal particles.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles are intermediate in size between those of a true solution and a suspension.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the intermediate-size description or a suitable size range.

rubric.why: Checks the optical property of colloids.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles scatter a beam of light (the Tyndall effect).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

rubric.why: Checks a further characteristic of colloidal particles.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles do not settle on standing or pass through ordinary filter paper but not a semipermeable membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either valid characteristic.

modelAnswer: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture, although it may appear homogeneous to the naked eye.
Its particles are intermediate in size between particles in a true solution and those in a suspension.
Colloidal particles scatter light, making the path of a light beam visible; this is called the Tyndall effect.
The particles do not settle on standing and pass through ordinary filter paper.

items.followUp: Differentiate between physical chemistry and biochemistry.

rubric.why: Checks the subject matter of organic chemistry.
rubric.description: Defines organic chemistry as the study of carbon compounds, especially hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the carbon-compounds distinction.

rubric.why: Checks the subject matter of inorganic chemistry.
rubric.description: Defines inorganic chemistry as the study of the compounds of the other elements, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the inorganic distinction.

modelAnswer: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals mainly with carbon compounds, especially hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
Inorganic chemistry deals with the compounds of the other elements, generally excluding most carbon compounds.

items.followUp: What does a chemical formula show?

rubric.why: Checks the shorthand function of an element symbol.
rubric.description: States that a symbol is a brief or shorthand representation of an element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

rubric.why: Checks the quantitative significance of a symbol.
rubric.description: States that a symbol represents one atom of that element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

modelAnswer: A symbol is a short-hand representation of an element.
It also represents one atom of that element.

items.followUp: Define isotopes and write the isotopes of chlorine.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of isotopes.
rubric.description: Defines isotopes as atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

rubric.why: Checks the names or symbols of hydrogen's isotopes.
rubric.description: Names the three isotopes of hydrogen: protium, deuterium, and tritium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for all three names or their correct isotope symbols.

modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
The three isotopes of hydrogen are protium (¹H), deuterium (²H), and tritium (³H).

items.followUp: Which radioactive isotope is used to study the thyroid gland, and what is its use?

rubric.why: Checks identification of the isotope used for the thyroid.
rubric.description: Identifies iodine-131 as the radioactive isotope used in diagnosing goiter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

rubric.why: Checks how the isotope helps with diagnosis.
rubric.description: Explains that the uptake or distribution of radioactive iodine in the thyroid is measured to help diagnose goiter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark.

modelAnswer: Goiter can be diagnosed using radioactive iodine-131.
A small amount is administered, and its uptake or distribution in the thyroid gland is detected to assess the gland.
